The university has a combined undergraduate and graduate student population of around 21,600.[[2]](#cite_note-verwaltung.uni-freiburg.de-2) About 16% of these students are foreigners, from about 120 countries. Admission largely depends on the faculty and program applied for and is strictly merit based, with the average score of final secondary-school examinations (German *[Abitur](/wiki/Abitur "Abitur")*) or A-levels playing an important role. Overall, in the fall of 2010, roughly 4,000 of around 26,000 applicants were admitted: this means that the university's acceptance rate that year was equal to 15.38%.[[9]](#cite_note-9)

The University of Freiburg offers a large variety of undergraduate, [graduate](/wiki/Graduate_school "Graduate school"), and [postdoctoral](/wiki/Postdoctoral "Postdoctoral") degree programs at its 11 faculties in 150 fields of study.[[10]](#cite_note-10)

As common among German universities, the academic year consists of summer and winter terms (semesters). The winter term runs from 1 October to 31 March, while the summer term runs from 1 April to 30 September. However, lectures and classes usually do not run for the full duration of these periods and allow for breaks in spring and fall.

As a German university, tuition is mostly free. The University of Freiburg currently has a semester fee of 180 EUR for all undergraduate and most graduate and doctoral programs. Additionally, since autumn 2017, non-EU students are charged 1500 EUR tuition fee per semester.[[11]](#cite_note-11)

The precise etymology of "Bhutan" is unknown, although it is likely to derive from the [Tibetan](/wiki/Old_Tibetan "Old Tibetan") [endonym](/wiki/Endonym "Endonym") "Böd" for [Tibet](/wiki/Tibet "Tibet"). Traditionally, it is taken to be a transcription of the [Sanskrit](/wiki/Sanskrit "Sanskrit") *Bhoṭa-anta* (भोट-अन्त) "end of [Tibet](/wiki/Tibet "Tibet")" through [Nepali](/wiki/Nepali_language "Nepali language") *Bhuṭān* (भुटान), a reference to Bhutan's position as the southern extremity of the Tibetan plateau and culture.[[25]](#cite_note-28)[[26]](#cite_note-Names&Histories-29)[[27]](#cite_note-lcweb2.loc.gov-30)

Since the 17th century, Bhutan's official name has been *Druk yul* (literally, "country of the [Drukpa Lineage](/wiki/Drukpa_Lineage "Drukpa Lineage")" or "the Land of the Thunder Dragon", a reference to the country's dominant Buddhist sect); "Bhutan" appears only in English-language official correspondence.[[27]](#cite_note-lcweb2.loc.gov-30) The terms for the Kings of Bhutan *Druk Gyalpo* ("Dragon King"), and the Bhutanese [endonym](/wiki/Endonym "Endonym") *Drukpa*, "Dragon people", are similarly derived.[[28]](#cite_note-31)

Names similar to Bhutan—including Bohtan, Buhtan, Bottanthis, Bottan and Bottanter—began to appear in Europe around the 1580s. [Jean-Baptiste Tavernier](/wiki/Jean-Baptiste_Tavernier "Jean-Baptiste Tavernier")'s 1676 *Six Voyages* is the first to record the name *Boutan*. However, these names seem to have referred not to modern Bhutan but to the [Kingdom of Tibet](/wiki/Tibet_(1912%E2%80%9351) "Tibet (1912–51)"). The modern distinction between the two did not begin until well into the Scottish explorer [George Bogle](/wiki/George_Bogle_(diplomat) "George Bogle (diplomat)")'s 1774 expedition. Google uses various [tax avoidance](/wiki/Tax_avoidance "Tax avoidance") strategies. On the [list of largest technology companies by revenue](/wiki/List_of_largest_technology_companies_by_revenue "List of largest technology companies by revenue"), it pays the lowest taxes to the countries of origin of its revenues.
